title: Augmenting Trends
text: trendseries comes useful datasets, presented vignette. electric dataset contains monthly electric consumption Brazilian households 1979 2025.  estimate trend use augment_trends select method: case, STL (see stats::stl). date_col (default "date") value_col (default "value") arguments identify relevant columns. result appended column named trend_{method} “trend_stl”, “trend_ma” (Moving Average), “trend_median” (Moving Median), etc. augment_trends best try infer appropriate frequency information can supplied manually. two options visualize data using ggplot2. first convert data “long” format define “name” series. default approach.  alternative add trend additional geom_line layer. quicker doesn’t scale well.
code: head(electric) #> # A tibble: 6 × 2 #>   date       consumption #>   <date>           <dbl> #> 1 1979-02-01        1647 #> 2 1979-03-01        1736 #> 3 1979-04-01        1681 #> 4 1979-05-01        1757 #> 5 1979-06-01        1689 #> 6 1979-07-01        1730  ggplot(electric, aes(date, consumption)) +   geom_line(lwd = 0.7) +   theme_series elec_trend <- augment_trends(   electric,   date_col = "date",   value_col = "consumption",   methods = "stl" )  head(elec_trend) #> # A tibble: 6 × 3 #>   date       consumption trend_stl #>   <date>           <dbl>     <dbl> #> 1 1979-02-01        1647     1675. #> 2 1979-03-01        1736     1695. #> 3 1979-04-01        1681     1716. #> 4 1979-05-01        1757     1731. #> 5 1979-06-01        1689     1747. #> 6 1979-07-01        1730     1761. elec_trend <- augment_trends(   electric,   date_col = "date",   value_col = "consumption",   methods = "stl",   frequency = 12 ) # Prepare data for plotting plot_data <- elec_trend |>   tidyr::pivot_longer(     cols = -date,     names_to = "series",     values_to = "value"   ) |>   mutate(     series = case_when(       series == "consumption" ~ "Data (original)",       series == "trend_stl" ~ "Trend (STL)"     )   )  # Create the plot ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = date, y = value, color = series)) +   geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +   labs(     title = "Residential Electricity Consumption",     x = NULL,     y = "Electric Consumption (GWh)",     color = NULL   ) +   theme_series ggplot(elec_trend, aes(x = date)) +   geom_line(     aes(y = consumption, color = "Original"),     linewidth = 0.7,     alpha = 0.5   ) +   geom_line(     aes(y = trend_stl, color = "Trend (STL)"),     linewidth = 1   ) +   scale_color_manual(values = c("#1E3A5F", "#1E3A5F")) +   labs(     title = "Residential Electricity Consumption",     subtitle = "Decomposition using an STL trend",     x = NULL,     y = "Electric Consumption (GWh)",     color = NULL   ) +   theme_series

title: Augmenting Trends
text: Filter-extraction methods spread across different packages thus use different conventions parameter names. trendseries tries simplify possible. Methods like moving averages moving medians shared “window” argument defines size rolling window. case STL, “window” argument inferred seasonal windows (.e. s.window).  Note trendseries simplifies trend extraction cost precision. noted , stats::stl t.window s.window argument. window argument trendseries controls s.window default.

what: How does augment_trends() compare to the traditional workflow?
title: Augmenting Trends
text: typical workflow estimating trends single series involves: Converting pairs date numeric columns ts objects. usually means manually inputting frequency start parameters. Applying filter function ts object. Extracting trend. Since filtering function returns different type object complexity varies. example stats::stl requires .$time.series[, "trend"] returns ts object. Converting ts object back original data.frame. can cumbersome, especially working multiple series grouped data. Merging back results original data can also error-prone due misalignment dates additional NA values introduced filters. instance, consider estimating HP filter gdp_construction. first step requires converting data frame ts object, manually inputting frequency start parameters. applying HP filter using mFilter package. finally, converting back data.frame merging original data. augment_trends() collapses four steps single call:
code: gdp_cons <- ts(   gdp_construction$index,   frequency = 4,   start = c(1996, 1) )  # Or, using lubridate to extract year and month gdp_cons <- ts(   gdp_construction$index,   frequency = 4,   start = c(     lubridate::year(min(gdp_construction$date)),     lubridate::quarter(min(gdp_construction$date))   ) ) gdp_trend_hp <- mFilter::hpfilter(gdp_cons, 1600) # Convert back to data frame using tsbox trend_df <- tsbox::ts_df(gdp_trend_hp$trend) names(trend_df) <- c("date", "trend_hp")  # Join with original data gdp_manual <- left_join(gdp_construction, trend_df, by = "date") gdp_auto <- augment_trends(   gdp_construction,   value_col = "index",   methods = "hp" )

text: closest alternative trendseries tsibble/fable ecosystem, provides model() function applying models — including trend extraction methods — grouped time series. Like trendseries, packages integrate well tidyverse tools pipes. However, fable designed primarily forecasting, means trend extraction capabilities limited. also lack popular methods commonly used economists, HP filter Hamilton filter. Additionally, packages require using tsibble data structure, pulls users away familiar data.frame/tibble format. users working just time series relying R’s built-ts functionality, tsibble structure can feel unnecessarily complex.

Often, though, economic series naturally described sum three parts: slow-moving trend, repeating seasonal pattern, irregular remainder. decompose_series() splits series three components adds columns original data frame. theme used throughout vignette consistent styling.

title: Decomposing Series
text: augment_trends() returns trend (trend_* columns). seasonal irregular movements smoothed away. decompose_series() returns trend, seasonal, remainder components (trend_*, seasonal_*, remainder_*), add back original series. seasonal component, decompose_series() requires seasonal data: monthly (frequency = 12) quarterly (frequency = 4). annual series nothing seasonal isolate, use augment_trends() instead.

title: Decomposing Series
text: Let’s start gdp_construction dataset, quarterly index Brazilian construction activity ships trendseries.  Passing data decompose_series() adds three new columns. frequency detected automatically date column. three components named method (stl default): trend_stl, seasonal_stl, remainder_stl. Reshaping long format makes easy plot original series alongside three components.
code: ggplot(gdp_construction, aes(date, index)) +   geom_line(lwd = 0.7) +   scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +   labs(     title = "Brazilian construction activity",     y = "Index"   ) +   theme_series gdp_parts <- gdp_construction |>   decompose_series(value_col = "index")  gdp_parts #> # A tibble: 124 × 5 #>    date       index trend_stl seasonal_stl remainder_stl #>    <date>     <dbl>     <dbl>        <dbl>         <dbl> #>  1 1995-01-01 100       102.         -4.37         1.93  #>  2 1995-04-01 100       101.         -1.62         0.476 #>  3 1995-07-01 100       100.          4.44        -4.62  #>  4 1995-10-01 100        99.4         1.55        -0.946 #>  5 1996-01-01  97.8     101.         -4.37         1.42  #>  6 1996-04-01 101.      102.         -1.62         0.613 #>  7 1996-07-01 107.      103.          4.44         0.370 #>  8 1996-10-01 103.      104.          1.55        -2.49  #>  9 1997-01-01 101.      106.         -4.37        -0.530 #> 10 1997-04-01 108.      109.         -1.62         0.849 #> # ℹ 114 more rows gdp_long <- gdp_parts |>   pivot_longer(     cols = c(index, trend_stl, seasonal_stl, remainder_stl),     names_to = "component",     values_to = "value"   ) |>   mutate(     component = factor(       component,       levels = c("index", "trend_stl", "seasonal_stl", "remainder_stl"),       labels = c("Observed", "Trend", "Seasonal", "Remainder")     )   ) ggplot(gdp_long, aes(date, value)) +   geom_line(aes(color = component), lwd = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +   facet_wrap(vars(component), ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +   scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +   labs(     title = "STL decomposition of construction activity",     subtitle = "Observed = Trend + Seasonal + Remainder",     y = NULL   ) +   theme_series

title: Decomposing Series
text: default method STL (Seasonal-Trend decomposition via Loess), implemented stats::stl(). seasonal component estimated loess smoother, trend adaptive moving average, remainder whatever left . defaults (s.window = "periodic", robust = FALSE) assume stable seasonal pattern. params list gives finer control. Two common adjustments evolving seasonal pattern robust fitting. s.window "periodic" forces identical seasonal shape every year; supplying positive odd integer instead lets shape drift gradually. Setting robust = TRUE reduces influence one-spikes trend seasonal estimates.
code: # Allow the seasonal pattern to evolve slowly over time, and downweight outliers gdp_robust <- gdp_construction |>   decompose_series(     value_col = "index",     params = list(s.window = 13, robust = TRUE)   )

title: Decomposing Series
text: regression method (methods = "regression") fits single OLS model yt=f(t)+s(t)+ϵt y_t = f(t) + s(t) + \epsilon_t f(t)f(t) polynomial time s(t)s(t) set period (month quarter) dummy variables. trend constant plus polynomial terms, seasonal component period effect (centred mean zero), remainder model residual. Unlike STL, regression trend smooth global polynomial, can better description series steady long-run direction. examples follow use oil_derivatives dataset, records monthly petroleum-derivatives production Brazil; restrict 1995–2006 window work log scale.  trend argument selects polynomial form: "linear" (default), "quadratic", "cubic". Orthogonal polynomials used default numerical stability.  series trend-stationary, remainder_regression — series trend seasonality removed — approximately stationary.  Comparing two methods directly, produce fixed seasonal patterns, STL follows short-term fluctuations closely, producing “cleaner” remainder.
code: suboil <- oil_derivatives |>   filter(between(date, as.Date("1995-06-01"), as.Date("2006-12-01"))) |>   mutate(lprod = log(production))  ggplot(suboil, aes(date, lprod)) +   geom_line(lwd = 0.7) +   labs(     title = "Petroleum derivatives production",     y = "Thousand barrels per day (log scale)"   ) +   theme_series suboil_reg <- suboil |>   decompose_series(     value_col = "lprod",     methods = "regression",     trend = "cubic"   )  ggplot(suboil_reg, aes(date)) +   geom_line(aes(y = lprod, color = "Original"), lwd = 0.7) +   geom_line(aes(y = trend_regression, color = "Trend (reg.)"), lwd = 0.7) +   labs(title = "Regression cubic trend", y = "log production", color = NULL) +   theme_series ggplot(suboil_reg, aes(date, remainder_regression)) +   geom_line(lwd = 0.7) +   labs(title = "Regression remainder", y = NULL) +   theme_series comparison <- suboil |>   decompose_series(value_col = "lprod", methods = "stl") |>   decompose_series(value_col = "lprod", methods = "regression", trend = "cubic")  comparison_long <- comparison |>   pivot_longer(     cols = trend_stl:remainder_regression,     names_pattern = "(.*)_(.*)",     names_to = c("component", "method"),     values_to = "trend"   ) |>   mutate(     component = factor(component, levels = c("trend", "seasonal", "remainder"))   )  ggplot(comparison_long, aes(date, trend)) +   # Original series   geom_line(     data = suboil,     aes(y = lprod),     layout = c(1, 2),     lwd = 0.5,     alpha = 0.5   ) +   # Components and methods   geom_line(aes(y = trend, color = component), lwd = 0.7) +   facet_grid(vars(component), vars(method), scales = "free_y") +   guides(color = "none") +   labs(title = "STL vs regression decomposition", y = NULL) +   theme_series

title: Decomposing Series
text: far handled multiplicative seasonality logging series decomposing (lprod = log(production), lvalue = log(value)). Many macroeconomic series behave way: seasonal variations grow level series, additive decomposition raw data leave seasonal pattern widens time. Every decompose_series() method additive construction. Instead logging manually, can pass transform = "log", logs series, decomposes additively, exponentiates components back original scale. decomposition additive log scale, exponentiating components multiply back series: trend * seasonal * remainder = value. requires strictly positive data.
code: decompose_series(   oil_derivatives,   value_col = "production",   transform = "log" )

title: Decomposing Series
text: methods = "classic" textbook decomposition implemented stats::decompose(). trend centred moving average order equal frequency, seasonal component average detrended value period, remainder left. simple fast, methods handle evolving seasonality endpoints better.
code: decompose_series(   oil_derivatives,   value_col = "production",   methods = "classic",   transform = "log" )

title: Decomposing Series
text: methods = "bsm" fits Basic Structural (state-space) Model stats::StructTS(): stochastic level, slope, seasonal components estimated maximum likelihood extracted Kalman smoother. Unlike moving-average methods, returns trend seasonal estimates every observation lets components evolve time. trade-relies numerical optimisation, can occasionally fail converge short irregular series.
code: decompose_series(   suboil,   value_col = "lprod",   methods = "bsm" )

title: Decomposing Series
text: methods = "seats" runs U.S. Census Bureau’s X-13ARIMA-SEATS program seasonal package — seasonal-adjustment procedure used many statistical agencies. seas() called automatic defaults: ARIMA model selection, log/level transformation, outlier detection, calendar adjustment. SEATS trend-cycle seasonally adjusted series mapped additive trend/seasonal/remainder triple. X-13 selects transformation internally, normally need set transform = "log" method. method requires seasonal package installed.   Often interest mainly series without seasonal component. convenience, deseason_series() wraps decompose_series() returns seasonally adjusted series directly.  equivalent using seasadj = TRUE decompose_series().
code: # requires the 'seasonal' package seas_oil <- decompose_series(   suboil,   value_col = "lprod",   methods = "seats" )  ggplot(seas_oil, aes(date)) +   geom_line(aes(y = lprod, color = "Original"), lwd = 0.7) +   geom_line(aes(y = trend_seats, color = "Trend (SEATS)"), lwd = 0.7) +   labs(title = "SEATS trend-cycle", y = "log production", color = NULL) +   theme_series ggplot(seas_oil, aes(date, seasonal_seats)) +   geom_line(lwd = 0.7) +   labs(title = "SEATS seasonal component", y = NULL) +   theme_series deseas_oil <- deseason_series(   suboil,   value_col = "lprod",   methods = "seats",   # set to TRUE to also return the trend, seasonal, and remainder components   components = FALSE )  ggplot(deseas_oil, aes(date, seasadj_seats)) +   geom_line(lwd = 0.7) +   labs(     title = "SEATS seasonally adjusted series",     y = "log production"   ) +   theme_series decompose_series(   suboil,   value_col = "lprod",   methods = "seats",   seasadj = TRUE )

title: Decomposing Series
text: decompose_series() splits seasonal (monthly quarterly) series trend, seasonal, remainder components, sum back original series. methods available "stl" (default), "regression", "classic", "bsm", "seats". methods additive; use transform = "log" multiplicative seasonality, components instead multiply back series. deseason_series() convenience wrapper returns seasonally adjusted series.

title: Detrending Series
text: Let’s start ibcbr dataset, monthly index Brazilian economic activity (IBC-Br) compiled Central Bank.  Passing data detrend_series() adds single new column, detrend_hp, holding deviation HP trend. frequency detected automatically date column.  big picture fairly correct: 2008–09 recession, 2015–16 crisis, COVID collapse show deep negative deviations. line also covered regular saw-tooth pattern. isn’t business cycle: ’s seasonality, points important caveat.

title: Econometric Filters
text: Henderson filter trend estimator inside official seasonal adjustment programs X-11, X-13ARIMA-SEATS (US Census Bureau), Statistics Canada’s X-12-ARIMA. Robert Henderson (1916) proposed smooth actuarial mortality tables, became standard national accounts trend extraction. Two properties explain . Cubic polynomial reproduction. filter passes polynomials degree 3 exactly — cubic trend returned unchanged. means filter distort smooth, polynomial-like economic trajectories. Minimum roughness. Among symmetric filters reproduce cubic polynomials, Henderson weights minimise sum squared third differences smoothed series, ∑t(Δ3τ̂t)2\sum_t (\Delta^3 \hat{\tau}_t)^2. Minimising third differences equivalent finding “gradually changing” trend consistent cubic-reproduction constraint.

text: filter length n=2m+1n = 2m + 1, unnormalized weights wj∝[(m+1)2−j2][(m+2)2−j2][(m+3)2−j2]⋅(η−j2),j=−m,…,m w_j \propto \bigl[(m+1)^2-j^2\bigr]\bigl[(m+2)^2-j^2\bigr]\bigl[(m+3)^2-j^2\bigr]   \cdot (\eta - j^2), \quad j = -m, \ldots, m η\eta determined setting ∑jj2wj=0\sum_j j^2 w_j = 0, enforces cubic polynomial reproduction. weights normalized sum one. distinguishing feature weights take small negative values outermost positions. Rather amplifying peaks troughs, filter slightly downweights extreme observations relative center. property gives Henderson trend characteristic stability turning points.
code: # Compute 13-term Henderson weights from the closed-form formula n <- 13L m <- (n - 1L) / 2L j <- seq_len(n) - (m + 1L)  P <- ((m + 1L)^2L - j^2L) *      ((m + 2L)^2L - j^2L) *      ((m + 3L)^2L - j^2L)  eta    <- sum(j^4L * P) / sum(j^2L * P) w      <- P * (eta - j^2L) w      <- w / sum(w)  weights_df <- data.frame(lag = j, weight = w)  ggplot(weights_df, aes(lag, weight)) +   geom_col(aes(fill = weight > 0), width = 0.65, show.legend = FALSE) +   geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.4) +   scale_fill_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#e74c3c", "TRUE" = "#2c3e50")) +   scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-6, 6)) +   labs(     title    = "13-term Henderson Filter: Weight Profile",     subtitle = "Weights sum to 1; small negative values at the outer lags stabilise turning points",     x = "Lag (j)", y = "Weight"   ) +   theme_series

text: Hodrick-Prescott (HP) filter one widely used trend-extraction methods macroeconomics. finds trend {τt}\{\tau_t\} solves penalised least-squares problem min{τt}∑t=1T(yt−τt)2+λ∑t=2T−1(Δ2τt)2 \min_{\{\tau_t\}} \sum_{t=1}^{T}(y_t - \tau_t)^2   + \lambda \sum_{t=2}^{T-1}(\Delta^2 \tau_t)^2 Δ2τt=τt−2τt−1+τt−2\Delta^2 \tau_t = \tau_t - 2\tau_{t-1} + \tau_{t-2} second difference. smoothing parameter λ\lambda trades fit smoothness: larger values force τt\tau_t closer linear trend. standard values λ=1600\lambda = 1600 quarterly data λ=14400\lambda = 14400 monthly data. defaults typically produce smooth trends.

title: Econometric Filters
text: Hamilton (2018) proposed regression-based alternative specifically designed avoid HP filter’s shortcomings. idea regress value hh periods ahead pp lags current level: yt+h=α+β1yt+β2yt−1+⋯+βpyt−p+1+εt+h y_{t+h} = \alpha + \beta_1 y_t + \beta_2 y_{t-1} + \cdots + \beta_p y_{t-p+1} + \varepsilon_{t+h} fitted values ŷt+h\hat{y}_{t+h} serve trend estimate. residuals ε̂t+h\hat{\varepsilon}_{t+h} form cyclical component. Hamilton (2018) recommends two years ahead one year lags: h=24h = 24, p=12p = 12 monthly data h=8h = 8, p=4p = 4 quarterly data. quarterly data regression written full yt+8=α+β1yt+β2yt−1+β3yt−2+β4yt−3+εt+8 y_{t+8} = \alpha + \beta_1 y_t + \beta_2 y_{t-1} + \beta_3 y_{t-2} + \beta_4 y_{t-3} + \varepsilon_{t+8} defaults trendseries monthly quarterly series respectively. regressors require pp consecutive lags dependent variable requires hh forward observations, first h+p−1h + p - 1 observations trend estimate.  cyclical component — deviations series Hamilton trend — reveals business cycle estimated regression residuals.

title: Econometric Filters
text: key differences two filters become visible comparing side side. contrast HP filter, Hamilton trend shows variability — reacts faster structural changes exhibit smooth “gliding” behaviour HP produces near endpoints sample.  use Hamilton: Prefer endpoint problem HP concern (e.g., near real-time analysis), want trend exposed critiques Hamilton (2018). also easy interpret — trend projection future level onto past values. Limitations: first h+p−1h + p - 1 observations trend estimate (35 months default monthly settings, 11 quarters quarterly). Unlike HP filter, trend available way last observation sample.
code: hp_vs_ham <- ibcbr |>   filter(date >= as.Date("2010-01-01")) |>   augment_trends(     value_col = "index",     methods = c("hp", "hamilton"),     .quiet = TRUE   ) hp_ham_long <- hp_vs_ham |>   pivot_longer(     cols = c(trend_hp, trend_hamilton),     names_to = "filter",     values_to = "trend"   ) |>   mutate(     filter = recode(       filter,       trend_hp = "HP (λ = 14,400)",       trend_hamilton = "Hamilton (h = 24, p = 12)"     )   )  ggplot(hp_ham_long, aes(date, trend)) +   geom_line(     data = hp_vs_ham,     aes(y = index),     color = "gray70",     linewidth = 0.5   ) +   geom_line(color = "#2c3e50", linewidth = 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) +   facet_wrap(vars(filter), ncol = 2) +   scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +   labs(     title = "HP vs. Hamilton Filter on IBC-Br",     subtitle = "Gray = original series; HP is smoother, Hamilton reacts faster and avoids endpoint distortion",     x = NULL,     y = "Index"   ) +   theme_series

title: Decompose time series into trend, seasonal, and remainder components — decompose_series
text: data data.frame, tibble, data.table containing time series data. date_col Name date column. Defaults "date". Must class Date. value_col Name value column. Defaults "value". Must numeric. group_cols Optional grouping variables multiple time series. character vector column names. provided, decomposition applied independently group. methods Decomposition method(s). One "stl", "regression", "classic", "bsm", "seats". Default "stl". several methods supplied (e.g. c("stl", "classic")), one contributes trend_*, seasonal_*, remainder_* columns decompositions can compared side side. "stl": Seasonal-Trend decomposition via Loess (stats::stl()). "regression": joint OLS trend + seasonal-dummy model. "classic": classical decomposition via moving averages (stats::decompose()). "bsm": Basic Structural (state-space) Model via Kalman smoother (stats::StructTS()). "seats": X-13ARIMA-SEATS decomposition (requires seasonal package; see Details). trend methods = "regression" : polynomial form trend component. One "linear", "quadratic", "cubic". Ignored methods. Default "linear". transform Transformation applied series decomposition. One "none" (default, additive decomposition) "log". "log", series log-transformed, decomposed additively, components exponentiated back, yielding multiplicative decomposition. frequency frequency series. Supports 4 (quarterly) 12 (monthly). auto-detected specified. methods require frequency > 1. seasadj TRUE, also add seasadj_{method} column holding seasonally adjusted series (series seasonal component removed: trend + remainder additive decompositions, trend * remainder multiplicative ones). Default FALSE. params Optional list method-specific parameters fine control. Every parameter default, argument needed non-standard use cases. STL (methods = "stl"): s.window stl_s_window: seasonal smoothing window. Either "periodic" (default, assumes constant seasonal pattern) positive odd integer (larger values allow slowly evolving seasonality). t.window stl_t_window: trend smoothing window (odd integer, NULL let stats::stl() choose automatically — recommended default). robust stl_robust: logical. TRUE, uses robust fitting reduce influence outliers. Default FALSE. regression (methods = "regression"): poly_raw: logical. FALSE (default), uses orthogonal polynomials (numerically stable, recommended). TRUE, uses raw polynomials (interpretable coefficients, less stable degree >= 2). classic, bsm, seats take params. multiplicative seasonality method, use transform = "log". .quiet TRUE, suppress informational messages.

title: Decompose time series into trend, seasonal, and remainder components — decompose_series
text: tibble original columns plus, requested method, three new columns (fourth seasadj = TRUE): trend_{method}: estimated trend component. seasonal_{method}: estimated seasonal component. remainder_{method}: remains removing trend seasonal. seasadj_{method}: seasonally adjusted series (seasadj = TRUE). transform = "none" components add back series (value = trend + seasonal + remainder); transform = "log" multiply back (value = trend * seasonal * remainder). "classic" trend (hence remainder) NA first last frequency / 2 observations (centred moving average boundary support). Output rows ordered date within group; original row order preserved.

title: Decompose time series into trend, seasonal, and remainder components — decompose_series
text: Uses stats::stl() (Seasonal-Trend decomposition via Loess). seasonal component estimated loess smoother, trend adaptive moving average, remainder residual. defaults (s.window = "periodic", robust = FALSE) assume stable seasonal pattern.

title: Decompose time series into trend, seasonal, and remainder components — decompose_series
text: Fits joint OLS model: $$y_t = f(t) + s(t) + \epsilon_t$$ \(f(t)\) polynomial time \(s(t)\) captured period dummy variables (month quarter indicators). components isolated via stats::predict(type = "terms"): Trend: constant + polynomial terms (captures long-run level direction). Seasonal: period dummy terms, centred mean zero sample. Remainder: residuals full model. default, orthogonal polynomials (poly_raw = FALSE) used numerical stability, matters trend = "cubic".

title: Decompose time series into trend, seasonal, and remainder components — decompose_series
text: Uses stats::decompose(). trend centred moving average order equal frequency; seasonal component average detrended value period; remainder residual. Simple fast, methods handle evolving seasonality endpoints better.

title: Decompose time series into trend, seasonal, and remainder components — decompose_series
text: Uses stats::StructTS(type = "BSM"), state-space model stochastic level, slope, seasonal components estimated maximum likelihood extracted Kalman smoother (stats::tsSmooth()). Unlike moving-average methods produces trend seasonal estimates every observation, including endpoints, lets components evolve time. Fitting relies numerical optimisation can occasionally fail converge short irregular series.

title: Decompose time series into trend, seasonal, and remainder components — decompose_series
text: Uses seasonal package, wraps U.S. Census Bureau's X-13ARIMA-SEATS program. seas() run automatic defaults (model selection, log/level transformation, outlier detection, calendar adjustment), SEATS trend-cycle (s12) seasonally adjusted series (s11) mapped additive trend/seasonal/remainder, whichever transformation X-13 picked internally. X-13 picks transformation , seats best used default transform = "none"; outer log transform redundant.

text: data data.frame, tibble, data.table containing time series data. date_col Name date column. Defaults "date". Must class Date. value_col Name value column(s). Defaults "value". Must numeric. character vector length > 1 accepted; column detrended separately results named detrend_{method}_{col} (e.g. detrend_hp_consumption). group_cols Optional grouping variables multiple time series. Can character vector column names. methods Character vector trend methods used detrending. method supported augment_trends() accepted. Default "hp" (Hodrick-Prescott filter frequency-appropriate smoothing). several methods supplied, one contributes detrend_{method} column detrended series can compared side side. transform Transformation applied detrending. One : "none" (default): trend fitted raw series detrend = value - trend, units series. "log": trend fitted log series detrend = log(value) - log(trend), log deviation trend. Multiplied 100, approximately percentage deviation trend (convention output gaps). Requires strictly positive values. trend_{method} columns (components = TRUE) reported back units series. frequency frequency series. Supports 4 (quarterly) 12 (monthly). auto-detected specified. components FALSE (default), detrended detrend_{method} column added. TRUE, fitted trend_{method} column also kept. window Unified window/period parameter moving average methods; see augment_trends(). "ma", "median", "henderson", numeric vector accepted (e.g. c(6, 12)), adds one detrended column per window value (detrend_ma_6, detrend_ma_12, ...). smoothing Unified smoothing parameter smoothing methods (hp, loess, spline, ewma, kernel, kalman). hp: use large values (1600+) small values (0-1) get converted. title: Extract trends from time series objects — extract_trends
text: function focuses monthly (frequency = 12) quarterly (frequency = 4) economic data. uses established econometric methods appropriate defaults: HP Filter: lambda=1600 (quarterly), lambda=14400 (monthly). Supports two-sided one-sided (real-time) variants Baxter-King: Bandpass filter business cycles (6-32 quarters default) Christiano-Fitzgerald: Asymmetric bandpass filter Moving Average: Centered, frequency-appropriate windows STL: Seasonal-trend decomposition Loess: Local polynomial regression Spline: Smoothing splines Polynomial: Linear/polynomial trends Beveridge-Nelson: Permanent/transitory decomposition UCM: Unobserved Components Model (local level) Hamilton: Regression-based alternative HP filter Advanced MA: EWMA various implementations Kernel Smoother: Non-parametric regression various kernel functions Kalman Smoother: Adaptive filtering noisy time series Median Filter: Robust filtering using running medians remove outliers Gaussian Filter: Weighted average Gaussian (normal) density weights Parameter Usage Notes: HP Filter: Use hp_onesided=TRUE real-time analysis future data influence current estimates. One-sided filter appropriate nowcasting, policy analysis, avoiding look-ahead bias. Default two-sided filter optimal historical analysis. EWMA: Use either window (converted alpha = 2 / (window + 1)) smoothing (alpha parameter), Kalman: Use smoothing parameter params list fine control noise parameters Spline: Use spline_cv control cross-validation (NULL=none, TRUE=LOO-CV, FALSE=GCV) Polynomial: Use poly_raw=FALSE orthogonal polynomials (stable degree > 2) poly_raw=TRUE raw polynomials. Warning issued degree > 3 (overfitting risk). UCM: Choose model type - "level" (simplest), "trend" (time-varying slope), "BSM" (seasonal component, requires seasonal data)
